raw_response:
Six useful designs suggest a division between basic value rendering, locale-aware value services, and whole-message translation. The following applications to Rust are design inferences, not claims that any component was deployed or proved useful for this problem.

1. **ICU MessageFormat, verified in ICU 52.1** — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/unicode-org/icu/release-52-1/icu4j/main/classes/core/src/com/ibm/icu/text/MessageFormat.java
   A library-owned message interpreter with named or numbered placeholders and locale-driven plural/select branches could supply translated-message behavior without adding that grammar to Rust's built-in formatting. The tagged source supports locale-bearing constructors and message patterns obtained from resources. A Rust implementation or binding would still need resource loading, maintained locale data and integration with Rust values. The official release page, https://icu.unicode.org/download/52, dates version 52.1 to 2013-10-09, before the cutoff. The current ICU guide was also consulted, but its later recommendations were not backdated.

2. **GNU gettext: translate a template, then format its values** — https://www.gnu.org/software/gettext/manual/html_node/Plural-forms.html
   Selecting a translated template and plural form from an external catalog before interpolation cleanly separates localization decisions from basic value formatting. The manual's ngettext interface obtains the appropriate catalog entry using translator-specified plural rules, after which ordinary formatting supplies argument values. This supplies a concrete composition boundary, but it is not a universal grammatical engine: its missing-catalog fallback uses a two-form source-language convention. Rust would need to support runtime translated templates through a library or generated adapter. The exact date of this live manual revision is unknown; the older Boost.Locale documentation separately confirms use of this gettext-based model.

3. **Mozilla L20n: put language-specific logic in localization resources** — https://blog.mozilla.org/l10n/2012/03/29/l20n-examples-for-localizers/
   A localization-specific language lets translators express gender and plural rules in resource files without forcing application code or core format strings to encode every language's grammar. The application can request a message by identifier and provide contextual values, while individual locales supply the necessary grammatical selection. This is a stronger alternative to adding scattered localization flags to a general formatter. It also requires a dedicated parser, resource format and translator tooling. The primary article is dated 2012-03-29; it supplies design examples, not evidence of deployment or suitability for Rust.

4. **Boost.Locale 1.55.0: compose localization with ordinary output abstractions** — https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_55_0/libs/locale/doc/html/messages_formatting.html
   An optional library that composes gettext catalogs, delayed translation objects and explicit or stream-specific locale selection shows how localization can be layered onto ordinary output facilities. A deferred message can be translated when rendered, allowing the same logical message to target different locales. The Rust transfer would be the library boundary and explicit locale-bearing rendering behavior, with an idiomatic interface replacing C++ streams. Catalog management and formatting compatibility remain application and library responsibilities. The official release notes at https://www.boost.org/releases/1.55.0/ date this version to 2013-11-11.

5. **ECMA-402 first-edition Intl objects: isolate locale-aware services behind an API** — https://402.ecma-international.org/1.0/
   A separately specified internationalization API with locale-configured formatter objects offers a boundary for number, date and collation services independent of a language's basic formatting syntax. Its configured objects can be reused with explicit language preferences and options. This is a useful alternative when a language wants a defined internationalization API without embedding all choices in format-string grammar. The December 2012 edition does not supply full message translation or arbitrary grammatical rules, and its complementary standard-library model does not by itself establish that every service should be external.

6. **Babel 1.3: external catalog tooling plus CLDR-backed locale services** — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python-babel/babel/1.3/docs/intro.rst
   An external package that owns catalog extraction tooling and CLDR-backed formatting shows how substantial locale data and localization workflows can evolve outside a language core. Its historical introduction separates catalog handling and pluggable extraction from localized values and names, highlighting that usable localization involves a workflow as well as string syntax. Rust would need an equivalent package or bridge; this split alone does not cover every whole-message grammatical requirement. The tagged 1.3 documentation was opened, and https://babel.pocoo.org/en/stable/changelog.html explicitly dates version 1.3 to 2013-07-29. Current Babel documentation was recorded separately as later evidence.

Taken together, these sources support evaluating a small basic formatter alongside optional locale-service and message-localization libraries. The critical interface is how typed application values and explicit locale/context information reach translatable whole messages; removing partial core behavior would still require that extension path to remain practical. This is an inferred design direction, not a final decision about Rust.
